Paths: Part three met Wassily Leontief's input-output table. Here is the Island's, for eight sectors. Each row is a buyer; each column a seller. A row says where a sector's costs go: so much to energy, so much to transport, and the rest, in the last column, to the people who work in it. Retail, for example, spends a fifth of its costs on the goods factories make, and fifteen cents in the dollar on farms.

Draw the same table as a network. Each sector is a node, and an arrow runs from seller to buyer whenever an input is a large part of the buyer's costs. Energy sells to every sector, metals mostly to factories. And households buy mainly services and retail, almost nothing from the metal works. The question of this chapter: when households spend a dollar, how much of it ends up as sales of each sector, and along which paths?

Follow a dollar of household spending. Some of it goes straight to a sector: forty-five cents to services, twenty-eight to retail. But retail spends part of its dollar on factories, which spend part of theirs on metals, which buy energy. Each step is one more power of the matrix of input shares, and the sum of all the paths is Leontief's inverse. The result is each sector's sales per dollar of GDP, its Domar weight, after Evsey Domar. Services sell 0.64, mostly straight to households. Energy sells 0.25, and only a fifth of that goes to households directly: the rest travels along chains of one, two or more buyers. The weights add up to 1.90, not one, because sales count an input again every time it changes hands.

One more measure of where a sector sits. Count, on average, how many steps its sales travel before they reach a household. That is its upstreamness. Metals are three and a half steps away: ore becomes steel, steel becomes a part, the part becomes a machine. Retail is one step: it sells to us. It is tempting to think that a sector deep upstream, feeding everything, must matter most when it fails. The next chapter says that, to a first approximation, it does not.
Hulten: In 1978 Charles Hulten proved a result that makes the network disappear. If the economy is efficient, the change in real GDP from a small change in one sector's productivity is that change times the sector's Domar weight: its sales divided by GDP. That is all you need. Not how many sectors it supplies, not how far upstream it sits, not even its share of value added. Its sales summarize everything the network does with its output.

Check it on the Island. Lower each sector's productivity by ten percent, one at a time, and solve the whole network for its new prices and GDP. In grey, the sector's share of value added: the wages it pays, as a share of GDP. In gold, its Domar weight. And in red, the fall in GDP that the model actually computes. The red dots sit on the gold bars, every one. Energy adds only 14 percent of GDP itself, but sells 25 percent, and a ten percent fall in its productivity costs 2.5 percent of GDP: its sales, not its value added.

Why? Suppose energy's productivity rises by ten percent. Every unit of energy now takes ten percent less to make, so, in a competitive economy, it costs ten percent less. Every buyer, whether a factory or a farm or a household, saves ten percent of what it spends on energy. And the total spent on energy, by everyone, is energy's sales. It does not matter who buys it or how long the chain is: the saving is the same. But notice the small print. The theorem is about small shocks, in an efficient economy. Chapters four and five break each of those conditions, and with them the idea that a sector's sales tell you everything.
PlayIt: Chapter three. Play it: which failure costs most?

Your turn. A disaster takes two fifths of one sector's productivity for a year. For that year, firms cannot easily switch to other inputs. Which sector's failure should the Island fear most? A: energy, which sells to every sector and sits nearly three steps from the household. B: chips, which go into every machine and car. C: services, the biggest seller of all, mostly straight to households. D: retail, the last step before the household. Which costs the most GDP?

Here is what the Island computes. The bars are the loss of GDP for the year; the white lines are what Hulten's rule predicts from each sector's sales alone. C. Services cost 30 percent of GDP, far more than any other, because they are by far the largest seller: the network's links do not rescue the upstream sectors from being smaller. But look at energy. Its sales predict a loss of 11.8 percent; the model computes 15.4. When inputs are hard to replace, losing an input that everyone needs costs more than its sales share, and the gap grows with the size of the shock. So sales decide the ranking, and Hulten is a good first answer. The premium for being upstream and hard to replace is the second answer, and chapter five is about when it becomes the first.
Granular: Chapter four. Why shocks do not wash out.

Robert Lucas made the argument in 1977: an economy has millions of firms, and each one's good and bad years are its own, so they should cancel out. If every firm's sales swing by twelve percent a year, independently, GDP's growth is the average, and its standard deviation is twelve percent times the square root of the sum of squared sales shares. With equal firms that falls like one over the square root of their number: ten thousand firms, and the aggregate swing is 0.12 percent, nothing. But firms are not equal. Their sizes follow something close to Zipf's law, the largest twice the second, three times the third. Then the square root barely falls: with ten thousand firms the aggregate still swings by 1.6 percent, as much as a real business cycle. The ten largest firms make 30 percent of all sales, and their shocks are the economy's.

Here are forty simulated years of the Island's GDP growth, from nothing but firms' own shocks: no recession, no central bank, no oil price. With equal firms, the line is flat. With firms sized like real ones, it swings by a couple of percent, up and down, like a business cycle. Xavier Gabaix called this the granular hypothesis: the economy is made of grains, some of them large. He measured the surprises of the hundred largest American firms, their growth above or below their peers', and found that they account for about a third of the swings in output.

Big firms are one reason the shocks do not cancel. The shape of the network is another. Daron Acemoglu, Vasco Carvalho, Asuman Ozdaglar and Alireza Tahbaz-Salehi compared economies in which every sector sells the same amount to households but buys differently. In a ring, each sector supplies the next. Add sectors, and the volatility of GDP falls away like one over the square root of their number, as Lucas expected. In a star, one sector supplies all the others. Its sales grow with the economy, so its shocks never become small, and the volatility of GDP stops falling. Same shocks, same number of sectors: the shape of the network decides whether the law of large numbers works.
Nonlinear: Chapter five. Beyond Hulten: large shocks.

Hulten's theorem is a statement about small shocks. David Baqaee and Emmanuel Farhi asked what happens with large ones. On the Island, change energy's productivity by every amount from a severe loss to a healthy gain. Hulten's rule is a straight line through the origin, with slope equal to energy's sales share, a quarter. If firms can swap between inputs with an elasticity of one, the computed response lies exactly on it. If inputs are hard to substitute, as they are within a year, the curve bends down: a loss of seventy log points in energy costs 27 log points of GDP, not seventeen and a half. If inputs are easy to substitute, it bends the other way. And with complements the curve is not symmetric: a bad shock costs more than a good shock of the same size gains.

Why does the curve bend? Hulten's rule still holds at every point on it: the slope is always energy's current sales share. The second derivative is the change in that share. Plot the share. When inputs substitute at an elasticity of one, it never moves. When they are complements, energy grows scarce and dear, everyone still needs it, so spending on it rises: its share climbs from a quarter towards 0.60, and each further loss costs more than the last. The network matters again, through prices: a sector that everyone needs and nobody can replace becomes a bigger share of the economy exactly when it fails.

This is an old puzzle with a new answer. In 1973 the price of crude oil roughly quadrupled within a few months. Oil was a small share of rich countries' spending, and Hulten's arithmetic says a small sector cannot cost much. Yet recessions followed. Baqaee and Farhi showed that the second-order terms, which depend on elasticities of substitution and on the shape of the network, can dominate when the shock is large and the input is hard to replace. So the rule is: sales first, then substitution. A small sector can matter a great deal if nobody can do without it, and the shock is big. Which brings us back to Japan.
Chains: Back to the Island's three thousand firms, in five tiers, now with a disaster. 5 percent of them, on the coast, lose 40 percent of their output for a year. Their direct customers lose sales because a part is missing: 7.4 percent on average. Their customers' customers lose 1.2, and the loss fades within a few steps. Upstream, the hit firms' suppliers lose a buyer: 17.1 percent at one step, 9.2 at two. Counting only the hit firms, the Island loses 2.0 percent of its sales. With the links, it loses 7.6: most of the damage is done to firms the disaster never touched.

What makes a link carry a shock? Some inputs are specific: made to the buyer's design, a moulded part, a custom chip. If its maker is hit, there is no other supplier for months. Direct customers who bought something specific from a hit firm lose 16.7 percent of their sales. Customers who bought only generic inputs from it, steel, packaging, lose 5.3, and most of that through their other links. Make every input replaceable and the direct customers' loss falls to 4.4 percent, and the Island's total loss from 7.6 percent to 6.0. What the links carry depends on what flows along them.

The real economy has run this experiment several times. In Japan in 2011, firms linked to the disaster area lost sales whether the link ran upstream or downstream, and the loss reached firms several links away: about half a point of GDP growth in all. Jean-Noël Barrot and Julien Sauvagnat followed American firms hit by hurricanes, floods and earthquakes over several decades. Their customers' sales growth fell by about two percentage points, but only when the hit supplier made something specific. Christoph Boehm, Aaron Flaaen and Nitya Pandalai-Nayar looked at Japanese-owned plants in America after the earthquake: their output fell almost one for one with the parts they could no longer import, as if inputs could not be substituted at all. Floods in Thailand later in 2011, the shortage of chips in the pandemic: the same mechanism each time, and each time a surprise to those who had not mapped their suppliers' suppliers.
ORing: On the twenty-eighth of January 1986 the space shuttle Challenger broke apart seventy-three seconds after launch, because a rubber seal, an O-ring, failed in the cold. Thousands of parts worked; one did not. Michael Kremer built a theory of production on it. A product needs several tasks done right, and its value is the product of the chances that each is done right. Four workers who each get their task right ninety-nine times in a hundred make 0.96 of the perfect output. Swap one of them for a worker who gets it right sixty percent of the time, and output falls to 0.58. One weak link costs two fifths of everything. If output were the average of the four, it would cost a tenth.

Multiplication has a consequence for who works with whom. Take four hundred of the Island's workers, with skills spread like this, and form a hundred teams of four. Teams drawn at random produce 49.7 units. Put the best with the best and the worst with the worst, and they produce 55.3: 11 percent more from the same people, because a skilled worker's care is wasted beside a careless one. So skills are complements, and firms, cities and whole countries sort: the best engineers work together, and a country with a few weak links in its infrastructure or its courts drags down the value of everyone's skill.

And pay. If output added up skills, a worker ten percent less careful would earn ten percent less. In Kremer's sorted economy, wages rise with skill to the power of the team's size. A worker ten percent less careful earns about 34 percent less. Small differences in skill become large differences in pay, within countries and between them. The network here is the smallest possible: four people at one bench. But it already shows the theme of this part. When everyone depends on everyone, the weakest link sets the pace.
Banks: Banks lend to each other, so a bank's ability to pay depends on whether its debtors pay it. Four banks. A owes B eight; B owes C six; C owes four to A and four to D. Each also has some money of its own. The rule, from Larry Eisenberg and Thomas Noe: each bank pays what it owes if it can, and otherwise everything it has, shared among its creditors in proportion. A owes eight and has two; it pays what it can, 5.5. B receives that, adds its own three, and pays its six in full. C receives six, has one of its own, and can pay only 7 of the eight it owes, half to A and half to D. But that payment is part of what A has: so A's 5.5 depends on C's 7, which depends on B's, which depends on A's. The payments are a fixed point, the clearing vector, and Eisenberg and Noe showed how to find it: start from full payment and lower it until everyone's books balance.

Is it safer for banks to owe each other a little, or a lot to one? Daron Acemoglu, Asuman Ozdaglar and Alireza Tahbaz-Salehi worked it out. Ten banks, each owing ten in total, each with a cushion of one. In a ring, each bank owes the next. A loss at one bank passes to the next in line, and each extra unit of loss topples one more bank. In a complete network, each bank owes a little to all the others. Small losses are shared nine ways and absorbed: only the bank that was hit fails. But past a threshold, a loss of about 10 here, the same links carry it to everyone, and all ten fail at once. Robust yet fragile: the dense network is the safest for small shocks and the most dangerous for large ones.

The theory arrived with the crisis that needed it. On the fifteenth of September 2008 Lehman Brothers was allowed to fail. The next day the American government rescued the insurer AIG, which had sold protection to too many banks to be let go. Afterwards, the leaders of the G20 agreed that standard derivatives should pass through central counterparties: clearing houses that stand between every buyer and seller, a star network built on purpose. Supervisors now collect who owes whom among the largest banks, to see the network before the shock. And the catch, from chapter four: a star is only as safe as its centre. And Matthew Elliott, Benjamin Golub and Matthew Jackson showed the same two-sidedness in the number of counterparties: spreading exposures first connects the network and lets cascades travel, then, as it grows, insures the banks against one another.
Diffusion: Chapter ten. Diffusion: who to tell first.

Here is one of the Island's villages: two hundred households, each linked to its neighbours and to a few people further away, with six households that everyone knows. A lender arrives and can tell five households about its loans. Each round, every household that knows tells each of its contacts with a chance of about one in eight. On the left, it tells the five most central households; in the middle, five at random; on the right, the five least central. Watch eight rounds.
After eight rounds, in this run, the news has reached most of the village when it started at the centre, much of it when it started at random, and only a corner of it when it started at the edge.

Averaged over three hundred runs: starting from the most central households, 86 percent of the village knows after eight rounds; from households chosen at random, 63 percent; from the least central, 15. Same village, same five conversations. Where the news starts decides how far it goes. Centrality here is eigenvector centrality: you are central if your contacts are central.

This is not only a simulation. In Karnataka, in south India, a microfinance lender entering forty-three villages first invited local leaders, teachers, shopkeepers and the heads of savings groups to a meeting, and asked them to spread the word. Abhijit Banerjee, Arun Chandrasekhar, Esther Duflo and Matthew Jackson had surveyed the villages' networks beforehand. Where the leaders who heard first were more central, more households took up the loans. Later trials have seeded information through the people villagers themselves name as good at spreading news: a cheap way to find the centre of a network without mapping it.
KeyPlayer: Chapter eleven. Games on networks: the key player.

Some behaviour is contagious: studying, smoking, crime. Coralio Ballester, Antoni Calvó-Armengol and Yves Zenou wrote it as a game on a network. Each player chooses an effort, and the more effort their contacts put in, the more each wants to put in, by a factor delta for each link. Here are thirteen of the Island's teenagers: on the left, a popular one with seven friends who do not know each other; on the right, a tight group of five who all know each other, one of whom also knows the popular one. In equilibrium the hub, with eight links, puts in 5.2. The clique members, with four or five links each, put in more, 5.9 to 6.7, because their friends' friends are also their friends. Effort equals each player's Bonacich centrality: it counts links, and links of links, and so on, each further step discounted.

Now a policy question. You can remove one player, by persuading them, treating them, or arresting them. Whose removal cuts the group's total effort the most? Removing the hub, the one with most friends, cuts it by 36 percent. A follower, by 8. But the clique member who also knows the hub cuts it by 50 percent: more than another clique member, 41, and far more than the hub. The key player is the one whose removal changes the network most, and that is not simply the one with most links. Ballester, Calvó-Armengol and Zenou derived a centrality that finds them.

All of this assumes that effort really is contagious. Charles Manski called the difficulty the reflection problem: friends may behave alike because they influence each other, because they chose each other for being alike, or because they share a school and a teacher. From group averages alone, the three cannot be told apart. A network helps. A friend of your friend who is not your friend moves your friend but not you, except through your friend: Yann Bramoullé, Habiba Djebbari and Bernard Fortin turned that into an instrument. Or assign roommates or classmates at random, and the sorting goes away. The key-player policy is only as good as the evidence that the effort is contagious.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: granular shocks and substitution.

This part opens two Dials. The first: what share of the swings in aggregate output comes from firms' and industries' own shocks, rather than from shocks that hit everyone? Gabaix's granular residual, the hundred largest American firms: about a third. Andrew Foerster, Pierre-Daniel Sarte and Mark Watson, separating industries' own shocks from common ones in industrial production: about half, after the mid-1980s, when common shocks grew quieter. Enghin Atalay, letting the elasticities of substitution be estimated rather than set to one: at least half. And the Island, where the truth is planted at 0.34: Gabaix's method finds 0.27 in the typical forty-year history, because it sees only the largest hundred firms, with a wide spread from one history to the next. The status is contested: a third to more than half, depending on the years, the data, and above all on the elasticities, which is the second Dial.

The second: how easily can a firm swap one input for another within a year? An elasticity of one is the Cobb-Douglas case, where Hulten's rule is exact; zero is Leontief's fixed recipe. Atalay, from American industries' input shares and prices: between zero and about 0.15, depending on the specification. Boehm, Flaaen and Pandalai-Nayar, from the Japanese-owned plants after the earthquake: about 0.2 among materials. And the Island: from thirty years of its tables, 0.16, with the truth planted at 0.15. Settled within a range: in the short run, inputs are close to fixed proportions. That is why chapter five's curves bend, and why a disaster's cost depends on what flows along the links.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: fragile by design.

The frontier is the network that firms build for themselves. Matthew Elliott, Benjamin Golub and Matthew Leduc model a large economy in which every firm needs several essential inputs, here four, and keeps relationships with a few possible suppliers of each. Any relationship can fail, and a supplier delivers only if it can produce itself. With two suppliers of each input, production is high while relationships are very reliable. With three, or five, the economy tolerates weaker relationships. But look at the shape. As relationships weaken, production holds up, and then, at about 0.78 with three suppliers, it falls from 86 percent of firms to none. A small aggregate shock, a slight weakening of every link, can cause a collapse. Their result is that firms, insuring themselves just enough, tend to settle near the cliff's edge: fragile in equilibrium, though never efficiently so. More suppliers move the cliff; they do not remove it.

What remains open? Networks rewire: after a shock, firms change suppliers, so the network is an outcome, not a given. Ezra Oberfield, and Daron Acemoglu and Pablo Azar, have built models in which it is chosen. Resilience costs money: a second source, or a stock of parts, is paid for every year and used rarely, and its benefit is shared by everyone downstream. Part sixty-six takes that up for whole countries. Measurement is improving fast: tax invoices and payment records now show who supplies whom, firm by firm, in a growing number of countries. And the old difficulty remains: telling what travels along the links from what the linked simply share.
